extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing whether a patent specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph), including when amended/new claims are entitled to earlier filing or priority dates. Covers substantive factors, examiner burdens, applicant reply handling, and procedural contexts (e.g., priority/continuation practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession determination factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification shows that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include the level of skill and knowledge in the art; partial structure; physical and/or chemical properties; functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function; and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to conclude the inventor was in possession is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation with nature and maturity of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention and with the scientific and technological knowledge already in existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents and printed publications should be used to determine whether an art is mature and the level of skill. In mature, predictable arts a specification that discloses only a method of making and function often will not raise a written description question for claims present when originally filed. In emerging or unpredictable technologies, more evidence is required to show possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method/function disclosure vs product claims (including product-by-process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and its function may not be sufficient to support a product claim (other than a product-by-process claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the process has actually been used to produce the product, the written description requirement for a product-by-process claim is satisfied. The requirement may not be satisfied where it is not clear that the acts set forth in the specification can be performed, or that the product is produced by that process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial structure disclosure limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization may not be sufficient to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For chemical/biological inventions (e.g., genes), conception requires definition sufficient to distinguish the compound and describe how to obtain it (structure, method of preparation, physical/chemical properties, or other distinguishing characteristics). Defining solely by a principal biological property is generally insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species claim support (tests a/b/c)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to a species must meet required tests (e.g., reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or disclosure of identifying characteristics) to avoid rejection for lack of adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any species claim that does not meet the test described under at least one of the enumerated bases must be rejected as lacking adequate written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claim support via representative species or identifying characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement for a claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species by reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or by disclosure of identifying characteristics (structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics coupled with structure–function correlation), or combinations thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'representative number of species' must reflect the variation within the genus. Where substantial variation exists, describe a sufficient variety of species. Disclosure of only one species supports a genus claim only if the disclosure indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative number and unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a disclosed set of species is 'representative' depends on whether a person skilled in the art would recognize that the inventor possessed the necessary common attributes of the genus; in unpredictable arts, one species will often be insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If representative species are not adequately disclosed for a genus, the genus claim must be rejected. Examples: claims to broad antibody genera not supported by disclosure of a single structurally similar antibody when other types exist; conversely, some arts permit a single species to indicate the class if the disclosure clearly conveys that other species are encompassed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure–function correlation as sufficiency basis
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable structure–function correlation may support a genus where structural features that produce the claimed function are disclosed or are known in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such correlations may be established by the inventor's specification or may be known in the art at the filing date. When established, they can permit broader claims without disclosure of every species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of claims must be commensurate with disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification cannot support expansive claim language merely by clearly describing one embodiment of the thing claimed; the issue is whether a person skilled in the art would understand the inventor to have invented the invention as broadly claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification teaches only a particular method/embodiment and gives no reason to generalize, broad generic claims may be invalid under 35 U.S.C. 112. Case examples (e.g., LizardTech) illustrate claims invalidated when only one particular method was disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support required for new/amended claims and priority/benefit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or to be entitled to an earlier filing or priority date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 365, or 386, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an explicit limitation in a claim is not present in the written description whose benefit is sought, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation. If not supported, new/amended claims must be rejected or benefit/priority denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency standard for support
rubrics_metrics.description: Inherency can supply support only if extrinsic evidence makes clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherency may not be established by probabilities or possibilities; mere chance that a result may occur is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner burden and required findings for a written description rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A description as filed is presumed adequate; the examiner bears the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning to rebut that presumption and explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as describing the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rejecting a claim the examiner must set forth express findings of fact including: (A) identification of the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establishment of a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the filing time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments supportable by the original disclosure, mindful of the prohibition on new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling applicant reply and record reassessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant reply, the examiner must re-evaluate the written description issue in view of the whole record (amendments, arguments, evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record now demonstrates the written description is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If not satisfied, repeat the rejection, fully respond to rebuttal arguments, and thoroughly analyze any affidavits or evidence submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession test (standard phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective standard: 'does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed' (i.e., that the inventor was in possession of the invention as now claimed)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention, or by reduction to practice or disclosure that the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., drawings or structural formulas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal vs non-literal disclosure; prohibition on added matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of the claim need not be described literally in haec verba to satisfy the written description requirement; however, if a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed (a departure/addition/deletion), the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conclusions lead to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or denial of benefit of an earlier filing date as appropriate. Examiners should use new-matter objection procedures where applicable (see MPEP § 2163.06).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential elements must be claimed or supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must include all elements which the applicant has described as essential; if the originally filed disclosure does not provide support for each claim limitation, or if an element described as essential is omitted from the claim, the claim must be rejected or benefit/priority denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law supports rejection where an essential element described in the specification is not claimed or where new claims attempt to encompass subject matter not supported in the earlier disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete patentability determination and clear Office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all relevant statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103) and clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and their bases in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before imposing any rejection, review all proposed rejections to confirm correctness. The Office action should set forth reasons and, when possible, offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical procedural circumstances raising written description issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Common situations where written description questions arise include: amendments affecting a claim; reliance on the filing date of a parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120; and reliance on foreign priority or provisional filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In each context, the claims must be supported by the relevant earlier disclosure 'in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a)'. The guidance includes examples of courts evaluating 'ipsis verbis' disclosure, blaze marks, and other indicators of sufficient support for benefit/priority claims.
